item.title: Premier League finds Manchester City guilty of more than 100 financial charges: report
item.description: Manchester City has been found guilty of more than 100 Premier League financial charges spanning an eight-year period, with sanctions still to be decided.
item.content:encoded:
The Premier League has reportedly given Manchester City a major red card.

City has been found guilty of more than 100 financial charges that were brought by the league over an eight-year period, according to a report from The Athletic. The punishment has not been decided, and City is expected to appeal potential sanctions, according to the report.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023," City told The Athletic in a statement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In November 2018, German outlet Der Spiegel published internal emails from City that it claimed detailed schemes by the club to conceal the true sources of income in a bid to comply with Financial Fair Play regulations. City did not dispute the emails but declined to comment because they came from hackers.

The emails prompted a Premier League investigation. In March 2019, UEFA opened a formal investigation into whether City broke the rules.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In February 2020, City was banned from the Champions League for two seasons by UEFA for "serious breaches" of spending rules and failing to cooperate with investigators. City was also fined 30 million euros (then $33 million). City said UEFA’s investigation was "flawed" and announced plans to appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

In July 2020, the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned City’s ban but still imposed a 10 million-euro ($11.3 million) fine for lack of cooperation with investigators.

In 2023, City was referred to an independent commission by the Premier League, which alleged more than 100 breaches of financial rules by the club. City was accused of providing misleading information about its finances from 2009-18 and subsequently failing to cooperate with the league’s investigation. City said it was "surprised" by the allegations and claimed there was a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" to counter them.

City won the Premier League for the fifth time in six seasons after the charges were brought. On Friday, The Athletic reported that City was found guilty of all but one of the charges.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: 'Pioneer Woman' Ree Drummond's son arrested on drug, assault charges
item.description: "Pioneer Woman" Ree Drummond's foster son Jamar Goff was arrested at the University of Alabama Birmingham on drug possession and assault charges.
item.content:encoded:
"Pioneer Woman" Ree Drummond's foster son is facing legal trouble after getting arrested in Alabama.

According to an inmate record online, the 57-year-old TV personality's son, Jamar Goff, 23, was arrested on Sept. 15 while at the University of Alabama Birmingham and booked on charges of drug possession and 2nd degree assault on a police officer.

He is also being held on charges of possession of drug paraphernalia and for attempting to elude a police officer.

Goff is currently being held at Jefferson County Jail in Birmingham, Alabama on a $35,000 bond.

REALITY STAR'S SON, 15, INDICTED ON 7 COUNTS STEMMING FROM ALLEGED ASSAULT

Fox News Digital has reached out to representatives for Drummond.

According to court documents obtained by TMZ, officers responded to a call about a suspicious person on the campus, and later found Goff sleeping shirtless on a bench near a fountain.

When approached by officers, Goff allegedly told them he was on campus because he was waiting for someone who was going to sell him "ice," which TMZ notes the documents say is another way to refer to methamphetamine.

Initially, the officers let Goff go, but after learning he had a warrant out for his arrest, approached him again and tried to handcuff him, which is when he ran away and allegedly hit an officer with an open palm.

"The state agency that handles fostering has strict rules against posting about foster children on social media, which I get. item.title: Erika Kirk sounds off after long awaited university report on husband's assassination
item.description: A 158-page report reveals UVU security was insufficient for Charlie Kirk's outdoor event, with inconsistent policies and no camera monitoring.
item.content:encoded:
Utah Valley University has released a 158-page report into the circumstances surrounding the assassination of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk on campus last year, when he was shot and killed during a public speaking event in the school's central courtyard.

The report, conducted independently by the Lake Forest Group but commissioned and released by the school, identified 10 "key findings" aimed at improving security for future events and concluded that no one at UVU acted "in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others."

Among those key takeaways, the reviewers found that UVU's application of its own policies "was significantly inconsistent;" security was insufficient for a high-profile, outdoor event and that there was no one in the university police department assigned to monitor campus security cameras.

CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY ALLEGES UVU KNEW OF ROOFTOP SECURITY RISK BEFORE HIS ASSASSINATION: LEGAL FILING

The reviewers also recommended reevaluating staffing levels and training given the university's size and potential for risk.

KIRK FAMILY MAY HAVE PATH AROUND ARCHAIC LAW SHIELDING GOV'T IN POLICE CHIEF'S ALLEGED 'GOT YOU COVERED' TEXT

Read the full report:

One concern raised in the report is that while universities have established systems to identify and thwart internal threats since the 2007 Virginia Tech shooting, those measures weren't applicable in the Kirk case because accused assassin Tyler Robinson had no connection to the school.

The report also concluded a timeline of major events in the lead-up to Kirk's visit to UVU between July 10 and Sept. 9, 2025. Several "key decision points" were identified between Aug. 25 and the day of Kirk's murder on Sept. 10.

SURVEILLANCE VIDEO TIMELINE TRACKS ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ACROSS UVU CAMPUS BEFORE FATAL ROOFTOP SHOT

On Aug. 25, the outdoor courtyard location remained the event venue despite concerns from UVU officials about their ability to control it, according to the review. Two days later, the event was approved without a documented security assessment plan in place. Campus police and TPUSA security had their "first direct security coordination" on Sept. 3, a week before the event.

On Sept. 8, TPUSA organizers raised their concerns about rooftop access in the area above where Kirk would be speaking. The report states that UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long sent TPUSA's security supervisor Dan Flood a text stating "We got you covered," but the review claims that the text was "in reference to the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway."

Flood arrived in person on campus on Sept. 10 with the TPUSA security team.

"Dan Flood, TPUSA Security Supervisor, texted Chief Long advising that TPUSA security personnel had arrived on campus," the report reads. "Chief Long engaged in a series of text communications with Flood, to include several regarding individuals located on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway and the Fountain Courtyard area where a canopy would be set up where Kirk would be speaking. These text exchanges revealed the primary security focus for TPUSA was the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway above the canopy."

This account differs from language in the Kirk family's notice of claim against UVU, filed last week, which identified the Sorensen Center rooftop as an area of concern, not the Hall of Flags walkway.

The Hall of Flags walkway was closed for the event, but TPUSA security never met with university police face-to-face, according to the review.

CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: NEW UVU PRESIDENT SAYS IT WILL CONTINUE TO 'HOST THE FRAYS,' EMBRACE FREE SPEECH

Ultimately, prosecutors allege that Robinson climbed atop the Losee Center building, which is to the northeast of the courtyard, and took the fatal shot from there.

The Hall of Flags walkway is directly above where Kirk was speaking. The Sorenson Center is the building to the north. The Losee Center is to the northeast.

ALLEGED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S FINGERPRINTS, PALM PRINT FOUND NEAR ROOFTOP: REPORT

"This report reaffirms the facts we laid out in our Notice of Claim: that UVU security was woefully understaffed and unprepared to manage the obvious risks associated with an event of this nature," Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said in a statement to Fox News Digital Friday. "UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie."

As the family alleged last week, the University Police Chief Jeffrey Long allegedly told Turning Point USA organizers that "I got you covered" when they raised concerns about rooftop access above the courtyard where Kirk was ultimately shot and killed by a sniper.

HOW CHARLIE KIRK’S ASSASSINATION CHANGED THE WAY CONSERVATIVES APPROACH HOSTILE OPPONENTS

"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

A university spokesperson told Fox News that the school has no further comment beyond a statement released on behalf of UVU President Dr. Jon Anderson.

"September 10 will always be part of UVU’s history, but it will not define our future," he said. "Our responsibility is to care for our community, learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations. This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn."

item.title: NFL wife fires back at league over ridiculous 15k fine, Presidents Cup has no juice & CBS's Melanie Collins!
item.description: The final Friday of September brings Kristin Juszczyk and Kyle Juszczyk trolling Roger Goodell over the NFL's absurd $14,926 celebration fine.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Friday of September. It's true. I had to double-check it, but it's true.

We're six days away from October. Goodness. Weren't we just grilling burgers on Labor Day Monday? What happened here? Wild stuff.

The good news? October is, objectively speaking, the best month of the entire year. It's really not even close. MLB playoffs. Football in full swing. Hockey starts back up. Still no NBA.

The best. It's what I hope heaven is like.

On that note, welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Kristin Juszczyk teams up with her 49ers husband, Kyle, to send a stern message to Roger Goodell and the No Fun League (NFL).

NFL FINES PLAYER NICKNAMED 'JUICE' $14,926 FOR USING A DRINKING CELEBRATION, CALLING IT OFFENSIVE

What a stunt they pulled earlier this week. They have absolutely no shame. You'll see.

What else should we hit on today before we leave early because it's a Football Friday and there are five (!!!) college football games today?

I've got NFL on CBS sideline reporter Melanie Collins checking in before Week 3, Al Michaels didn't have the greatest night in the booth last night, and Wyndham Clark wasn't a fan of the ... fans ... at the Presidents Cup in Thursday's opening round.

I don't blame him, by the way. But also, this event ain't exactly the Ryder Cup. Never has been, and never will be. There's just no juice in it.

OK, grab you ... some juice! ... and settle in for a Friday 'Cap:

We ended yesterday's class with the dumbest story in the NFL ... maybe ever? For those who missed it, Roger Goodell's Fun Police fined 49ers FB Kyle Juszczyk a whopping $14,926 for celebrating a touchdown by giving the universal symbol of taking a drink.

The league took it as Juszczyk "chugging a beer," according to the letter sent to Juszczyk. That violates Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which, frankly, sounds like the dumbest rule of all time.

Anyway, the Niners star has been doing that celebration for years, and it has nothing to do with beer. He barely drinks beer. Instead, it's an homage to his nickname — "Juice."

By the way, as OutKick's Armando Salguero noted, Juszczyk scored the tuddy, did his VERY BAD celebration, and then the first commercial that appeared when FOX went to break?

A Michelob Ultra ad.

Amazing.

We all caught up now? Good! Now, let's check in with Kyle's wife, Kristin, who had her husband join her for an Instagram message to the league:

"Kyle’s got a drinking problem," the caption says, followed by the little nod to the league with the text in the video that reads, "$14,926 glass of juice."

Amazing. It really is a ridiculous fine by the league, and my bar for Goodell is already so low. The NFL has been the No Fun League for decades now. You can't celebrate. You can't taunt. You can't hit the QB. You can't touch the receiver. God forbid you jump on the goal posts after you score a touchdown.

I'm fairly certain that celebration is punishable by death at this point.

But this fine ... for a DRINKING GESTURE ... might just be the leader in the clubhouse. It's that silly. Especially when all the league promotes is drinking and gambling. That's literally every single commercial on NFL Sundays. That's it. Bud Light and Kalshi.

And Jason Kelce hosting a football party, of course. Can't forget that one.

Anyway, good for Kristin for fighting back. It pays to have an influencer wife, you know?

Yep. That works!

OK, let's move this class along and check in with Wyndham Clark and Team USA:

"It was kind of dead out there. I felt like the momentum could have been better, to be honest, because we weren’t really feeling the fans, I think, as much as normal. There was a few shots — I mean, Collin hit a 5-wood on, what was it, 11 to like 10 feet, and we didn’t even know if it was on the green because no one clapped. It was a little surprising."

I don't love Wyndham Clark, but it's tough to argue with him here. I said it on Monday ... I had NO idea the Presidents Cup was this week. None. Zero. It's been the least-hyped golf event of my lifetime.

They played all day yesterday and I didn't see one thing about it on social media. Not one. I know this has always been the little brother to the Ryder Cup, but it's been as bad as I can remember this year.

And now we're going into the weekend and putting it up against college football and the NFL? Good luck.

Not great!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big weekend. First up? How do we feel about Al's performance last night?

Thoughts?

The confusion on the "ATL" chants were wild, from both guys. How were they so bewildered by "ATL" chants ... when the ATLanta Falcons were playing? What do you guys think "ATL" means?! Feel like that one comes with some pretty easy context clues.

For me, the worst one was Al's call on Bijan Robinson's long run in the first quarter. I can look the other way on most of it. He is 81, after all.

But the lack of energy and enthusiasm on that run was a bad look. I get it's the first quarter, but come on. This is your big game of the week. You're in Primetime. All eyes are on you.

It wasn't his best. The good news? It's only Week 3. Come on, Al! Chin up, and let's turn this season around.

Next? On the way out, here's Doug Gottlieb going on what I thought was relatively solid 5-minute rant on the current state of college athletics:

I'm not the biggest Gottlieb fan, but I actually agree with a lot of what he says there. The free-for-all that is the transfer portal has gotten laughably out of control in college sports, specifically football and basketball. It's just insane. To me, that's the worst part of this whole NIL era we're suffering through right now.

I can stomach the ridiculous amounts of money being thrown at these 18-year-olds. But seeing a 23-year-old on his 5th team in as many years just ruins the whole experience.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Good work, everyone. Another weekend is here. Final one of September.

Let's end this month with a bang.

Take us home, NFL on CBS reporter, Melanie Collins!

item.title: Seattle startup gives FOX News firsthand look at AI-powered vehicles built for the Marines
item.description: Overland AI gives a firsthand look at autonomous ground vehicles being developed for the U.S. Marine Corps to support logistics and ammunition resupply in contested environments.
item.content:encoded:
From Ukraine to the Middle East, drones and other unmanned systems are playing an increasingly visible role in modern warfare. Nations are quickly competing to integrate AI tech into everyday military operations to eliminate human risk while improving overall efficiency in the field. 

One example of that development is based in Seattle, Washington. 

Late June, defense-tech company Overland AI announced it had secured a roughly $20 million dollar production contract with the U.S. Marine Corps for autonomous unmanned ground vehicles, or AUGVs, with delivery expected in early 2027. 

AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI - CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD

"This is a vote of confidence from the Marines that the technology that we have is ready for the mission," said Greg Okopal, Co-Founder and COO of Overland AI. 

The Marine Corps tells FOX the goal is to use the vehicles for missions such as moving ammunition and supplies while reducing risk to Marines.

The award came through APFIT, the Pentagon’s Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies program, using a production Other Transaction Agreement, or OTA. APFIT was started in fiscal year 2022 to help move proven technologies into military use faster. The program is designed to speed up production and shorten the procurement process, essentially helping cut through some of the red tape.

The tech is being developed to support the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, or MADIS, designed initially to focus on autonomous logistics, including ammunition resupply, in contested environments. Okopal says Overland’s work falls under the Marine Corps’ ground-based air defense program, "...which is really sort of a disparate array of vehicle-mounted sensors and effectors that can protect from various UAS (Unmanned Aerial System) and other airborne threats."

But why the investment in ground autonomy? 

Overland AI argues while aerial drones and other unmanned systems have become increasingly important on the battlefield, "wars are still won on the ground." Describing the growing role of unmanned or autonomous ground vehicles, Overland AI Chief of Staff Chris Merz pointed to Ukraine, where he says the technology is being used more and more for combat.

"They started with using them for sustainment but increasingly you're seeing them used in combat operations, taking and holding terrain…I really think that is the future application of uncrewed and autonomous ground vehicles and we'll start to see that more in future conflicts."

WATCH: EXCLUSIVE LOOK AT BLUE-COLLAR WORKFORCE FUELING AMERICA’S AI BOOM 

Unlike remotely operated ground vehicles, Overland's system is designed to navigate and execute missions fully autonomously, without a human continuously steering the vehicle or even controlling it remotely. "Our vehicles, you task them with a mission, you press execute, those vehicles will execute that mission whether you have communications with them or not, whether you're paying attention to them or not, they are fully autonomous," Okopal explained.

Overland says its vehicles can also operate beyond the line of sight and in GPS-denied environments, executing an assigned mission even when communications are unavailable. "All battlefields now are electronic, contested environments, right? So you cannot necessarily rely on distant comms to complete your mission," Okopal explained. 

TRUMP RENAMES AI ‘SUPERINTELLIGENCE,’ REJECTS ‘GLOBALIST’ CONTROL PLAN 

The vehicles are designed to perceive their surroundings and navigate off-road terrain, including obstacles such as ditches, inclines and boulders. Rather than solely directional focused capabilities, the AI technology behind it is more mission focused. For example, an entire fleet of vehicles can be programmed with the mission to establish surveillance and reconnaissance around specific coordinates, manage threat response, etc.

"The very important thing is getting Marines and soldiers for the Army as well out of danger," Okopal explained. 

The Marine Corps shared this statement with FOX:

"The U.S. Marine Corps Program Manager Ground-Based Air Defense (PM GBAD) has awarded an Other Transaction Authority (OTA) agreement to Overland AI to develop and procure Autonomous Unmanned Ground Vehicles (AUGVs). Designed to sustain the Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) family of systems across contested littoral and distributed operating environments, these AUGVs bridge the 'last tactical mile' logistics gap by automating ammunition resupply and reducing risk to warfighters. While initial efforts focus on autonomous logistics distribution via resilient, AI-driven networks, future capability spirals will integrate modular sensor packages and effectors to extend the active detection, tracking, identification, and defeat of unmanned aerial systems (UAS), rotary-wing aircraft, and low-altitude fixed-wing threats."

item.title: Leftist protester disrupts Climate Week event by ranting against US military
item.description: Code Pink disrupted a Nature Conservancy event at NYC Climate Week, demanding the group address the Pentagon's carbon footprint and military pollution.
item.content:encoded:
A member of Code Pink, the far-left group known for confronting elected officials, disrupted a Climate Week event in New York City Thursday, blaming the U.S. military for its perceived role in the climate crisis.

The disruption targeted an event hosted by The Nature Conservancy, which the group claims refuses to address the U.S. military’s "massive carbon footprint and massive environmental degradation from U.S. military bases and U.S.-driven wars and occupations."

"There is an elephant in the room that The Nature Conservancy does not want to address," said a man identified by Code Pink only as Aaron, the campaign organizer for the group's War Is Not Green initiative. "It is destroying ecosystems. It is destroying fish. It is destroying the world."

$54M CODEPINK-LINKED FOUNDATION SHUT DOWN IN CALIFORNIA POPS UP AT RAMSHACKLE MIAMI HOME

He also pointed to the Pentagon’s $1.5 trillion budget and the U.S. military’s role in environmental destruction, asking why The Nature Conservancy, with a budget of over $2 billion and a mission dedicated to protecting land and water, refuses to address it, the group said.

Code Pink said it was present at NYC Climate Week to insist that any serious climate conversation must include the military-industrial complex, which it argued contributes significantly to global warming.

INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE'

Code Pink demanded that The Nature Conservancy and other environmental groups "publicly acknowledge the U.S. military as a leading institutional polluter," "refuse partnerships or funding tied to the military-industrial complex" and "use their platforms to demand cuts to the Pentagon budget and an end to wars that devastate ecosystems."

"You cannot claim to protect the land and waters while ignoring the largest institutional polluter on Earth," Aaron explained after the disruption. "The Nature Conservancy has a $2 billion budget and a global platform. It has a responsibility to name the war machine as a driver of climate destruction. Silence is complicity."

Fox News Digital has reached out to The Nature Conservancy.

item.title: Brewery that offered free beer when Trump dies faces possible closure after state revokes alcohol permits
item.description: Minocqua Brewing Co.'s Madison taproom faces likely closure by year's end after Wisconsin officials revoked its alcohol permits over alleged violations.
item.content:encoded:
The owner of Minocqua Brewing Co. said Monday that the Madison taproom in Wisconsin will likely shut down by the end of the year after state officials revoked the company’s alcohol permits.

Channel 3000 reported that Minocqua Brewing Co. owner Kirk Bangstad said the Madison taproom is likely to shut down as the business continues fighting the state’s decision. 

The brewery has become known for its outspoken messaging against President Donald Trump.

WISCONSIN BREWERY THAT OFFERED 'FREE BEER' WHEN TRUMP DIES SAYS ALCOHOL PERMIT REVOKED

The Wisconsin Department of Revenue (DOR) revoked brewing permits for the company’s Minocqua and Madison locations after alleging violations involving beer transported from Illinois without the required permits and tax payments. The brewery has disputed the state’s action and accused officials of targeting it because of its political views.

The department told Fox News Digital in a statement Thursday that there is a hearing on the company's appeal on Nov. 18, and that the revocation does not take effect until appeals are done, adding that the "DOR is dedicated to fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverage regulations in Wisconsin and takes action when the laws are not followed, as occurred here."

Bangstad’s breweries have made headlines for offering free beer if President Trump dies.

On Jan. 22, the Minocqua Brewing Company appeared to suggest it would give free beer to patrons if Trump was killed, and while not explicitly using his name, posted on Facebook, "Free beer, all day long the day he dies."

'FREE BEER' FOR TRUMP DEATH DEM ACTIVIST RUNNING FOR WISCONSIN GOV: 'I WILL WIN' IF THEY SILENCE ME

"Show us this post when it happens in a few months and we’ll make good on that promise," the post continued. 

The post was updated to say, "We meant the Madison Taproom because that’s open all year, if he dies in the summer, then it’s gonna be the Minocqua Taproom."

In reply to comment on the post, the company also did not refer to Trump by name but said the message referred to a high-profile figure when asked whether the timeline for the deal could be moved up earlier.

After the April shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner where Trump was present, the company wrote on Facebook, "Well, we almost got #freebeerday."

KENTUCKY GOVERNOR SAYS HE RECEIVED 2 CALLS FROM AGENCIES INDICATING MCCONNELL HAD 'PASSED'

The brewery also offered half-price beer when Sen. Mitch McConnell dies.

"When they announce that McConnell’s Faustian dance has finally ended, we’re gonna start serving our beer at ‘half price,’ because we promised #halfpricebeerday on the day they unplug the ventilator," the brewery said in an Instagram post.

McConnell, who is 84, was absent from the Senate for months after being hospitalized for a fall in his home earlier this year. The Kentucky Republican returned to the Senate last week ahead of key votes. 

Bangstad, who owns the brewery, is also the founder of the Minocqua Brewing Company SuperPAC, which "aims to remove Republican federal and state elected officials who perpetuated the election lies that caused the Insurrection of January 6, 2021, and whose downplaying of the seriousness of COVID-19 caused so many unnecessary deaths in our country," according to the brewery’s website.

Reached for comment by Fox News Digital, the brewery made disparaging remarks about Trump and again noted that it will host a "#freebeerday" when the president passes. 

"Reminder, however, no red hats allowed," the brewery added.

item.title: New Jersey Lt Gov Dale Caldwell resigns after sexual harassment investigation
item.description: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned after an investigation substantiated sexual harassment and ethics violations, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Democrat New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned Friday after an independent investigation substantiated sexual harassment and ethics violations against him, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced.

"He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted," Sherrill said during a news conference in Trenton.

Sherrill had given Caldwell until Friday to resign after the investigation found he "failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office" and demonstrated a pattern of behavior that did not meet her administration’s standards.

NEW JERSEY GOV MIKIE SHERRILL CALLS ON LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR TO RESIGN AFTER SEXUAL HARASSMENT INVESTIGATION

The report found Caldwell told a female staffer that "you young women are looking for young sperm" after she told him her younger friend was not interested in a romantic relationship with him. Investigators concluded the remark constituted sexual harassment and found Caldwell’s denial that he made it was not credible.

Caldwell previously denied wrongdoing, calling the allegations false and misleading and saying he believed the facts would exonerate him.

item.title: Flyers forward Trevor Zegras slapped with one of the most ridiculous penalties of all time
item.description: Trevor Zegras was sent to the penalty box for tucking his jersey into his pants during the Philadelphia Flyers' preseason win over the Boston Bruins.
item.content:encoded:
The NHL is still working through its preseason, and already we have a candidate for the worst penalty of the year, and possibly ever.

The Philadelphia Flyers hosted the Boston Bruins in their penultimate tune-up before their season-opener against their arch-rivals, the Pittsburgh Penguins.

Now, the Broad Street Bullies came out on top in this one, 2-0, but that wasn't the story. Instead, all of the talk after the game had to do with Flyers forward Trevor Zegras getting a minor for delay of game for "improperly wearing equipment."

MLB TELLS UMPIRE DOUG EDDINGS HE MADE A MISTAKE IN DEMANDING CARDINALS PITCHER STRAIGHTEN HIS HAT

Zegras hopped over the boards to take a faceoff with the back of his jersey tucked into his pants. Most of us wouldn't think twice about it, but an official saw it and sent him to the sin bin.

That's because this season, officials have been told to crack down on players not wearing equipment properly, and technically, he was.

But that doesn't make it any less absurd.

MASSACHUSETTS YOUTH HOCKEY PLAYER SUSPENDED AFTER VICIOUS SLASHING INCIDENT GOES VIRAL

At the risk of sounding like a certain cartoon sports radio host, it used to be that tucking your sweater into your pants was the cool thing to do.

Well, not anymore.

According to The Athletic, Zegras confirmed after the game that he had been issued a warning before he was given the penalty, which is in line with the rulebook. Had he done it again, it would've been a game misconduct.

Head coach Rick Tocchet mentioned afterward that the league had given a heads-up about this push — which focuses on everything from visors to neck guards to, of course, jerseys — a few weeks earlier.

"They told us, in all fairness, two, three weeks ago," Tocchet said. "I didn’t even think about it. … Obviously, can’t do it anymore. Regular season starts, we can’t have a penalty like that. I actually had to put (forward Matvei Michkov’s jersey) down on the bench."

Hey, rules are rules... but nothing says preseason like the league picking a rule that never gets enforced to the point that most of us forgot it existed, and then dropping the hammer.

item.title: Airport X-ray reveals shocking illegal stash concealed beside passenger's Xbox
item.description: A checked bag alarm triggered by an Xbox at LaGuardia Airport in New York City led TSA officers to discover a plastic bag full of fraudulent IDs with matching photos.
item.content:encoded:
TSA officers recently made an unexpected find inside a passenger's checked bag after an Xbox triggered an alarm. 

The unusual discovery was announced by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA). 

The incident occurred this month as a passenger was moving through the TSA line at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in New York City when an alarm went off.

"The bag alarmed on an Xbox gaming system, and TSA Officer Ashley Leo, who was manning the on-screen resolution area, diverted the bag to the checked baggage resolution area, where Supervisory Transportation Security Officer (STSO) Christopher Ramos was stationed," the TSA said in a statement.

It's what Ramos found beside the Xbox that stood out.

As he searched through the bag, he discovered "a plastic bag containing several fake IDs next to the Xbox that prompted the alarm," according to the TSA.

"I noticed various driver’s licenses with different dates of birth and different class types, but all with the same photograph," Ramos said in a statement.

AIRPORT X-RAY SHOWS TERRIFYING OBJECT TAPED IN CARRY-ON TO SKIP CHECKED BAGGAGE FEE

"I was focused on following our screening procedures and paying close attention to anything that appeared unusual.

"When I discovered the fraudulent IDs, I knew it was important to report the situation through the proper channels."

After involving TSA management, airport officials and Port Authority police, authorities confirmed the IDs were fraudulent and arrested the passenger moments before he was scheduled to board his flight.

"STSO Christopher Ramos’ strict adherence to standard operating procedures, diligence and situational awareness prevented the fraudulent IDs from entering the airport’s secure area," TSA LGA Federal Security Director John Essig said in a statement.

"Identifying fraudulent IDs is an important part of TSA’s layered security approach. It helps ensure that people entering secure areas of the airport are who they claim to be and supports the safety of the traveling public."

item.title: Flying sports car hides its wings as production gets closer
item.description: Samson Sky's Switchblade flying car secures $80 million from Dubai's Matin Group, but the redesigned hybrid-electric aircraft still needs more testing.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever been stuck in traffic wishing your car could sprout wings, Samson Sky has been working on something pretty close. Its Switchblade flying car can drive out of your garage and take you to a nearby airport. Once there, the wings come out, the tail extends and the vehicle becomes an airplane. You heard right, an airplane. After landing, everything folds back inside so you can drive the rest of the way.

That idea has been around for years. What makes Switchblade worth another look right now is that Samson says it has secured an $80 million investment from Dubai-based Matin Group. Samson plans to use the funding to help move the project toward U.S. production. The company still needs another $20 million to fully fund its current production plan. That new backing gets the Switchblade closer. But what really caught my attention is how much Samson has changed since we first watched this flying car take off.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.

Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.

The latest Switchblade design looks much more like a car when you are using it on the road. Samson says the wings, tail and propeller are now fully enclosed inside the vehicle during driving mode. That is a major change from the earlier design that completed its first flight in November 2023. When you reach an airport, the wings extend and the tail moves into position for flight. Samson says the transformation from driving mode to flying mode takes about three minutes.

After you land, the process reverses. The flight hardware folds back inside the body before you continue the trip by road. Samson says that setup allows the Switchblade to fit inside a standard garage while also protecting the flight surfaces when the vehicle is being driven or stored. There is still a runway involved, though. The Switchblade does not take off vertically from your driveway. You drive it to an airport, transform it into flight mode and take off from there.

We first covered the Switchblade after its official first flight on Nov. 5, 2023. The prototype flew from Grant County International Airport in Moses Lake, Washington. Since then, Samson has kept working on the version it hopes to put into customers' hands. The company has changed the design and increased the size of its engine. Samson says it plans to use three production prototypes for more testing around the end of 2026 or beginning of 2027.

So while we have already seen a Switchblade get off the ground, the version heading toward production has changed since that 2023 flight. That is why I am especially interested in what happens next. I want to see the latest Switchblade take to the air and show us what this new design can actually do.

Samson is targeting some attention-grabbing performance numbers. The company currently lists a maximum airspeed of 190 mph and a maximum flying range of 450 miles. It lists a maximum road speed of 100 mph. Samson also lists a 160 mph cruise speed. However, its FAQ says that anticipated figure still needs verification during production-prototype flight testing.

The Switchblade uses a hybrid-electric drivetrain. A gasoline engine powers a generator, which supplies electricity to the vehicle's motors. Samson says the system powers the wheels on the ground and the propellers in flight. The company currently lists a 44-gallon fuel capacity and says the vehicle uses 91-octane automotive gasoline.

HELMET-STYLE COCKPIT VISION SYSTEM AIMS TO CHANGE HOW PILOTS SEE IN LOW VISIBILITY

Making a flying prototype and building vehicles for customers are two very different challenges. Samson says the new $80 million investment will help establish its first 180,000-square-foot Switchblade production facility in the U.S. The company signed a Joint Investment Agreement with Matin Group, and the two companies have started setting up a joint venture. Where that factory ends up remains an open question.

Samson Sky CEO and founder Sam Bousfield tells CyberGuy that the search has narrowed considerably, saying, "We will maintain our Samson Sky R&D Facility in Prineville, OR, and we have narrowed down the US production facility to three potential locations in different parts of the country, with some negotiations already begun." Samson has not identified those locations publicly. There is serious new money behind the production effort, but another financial hurdle remains. Samson says $20 million still needs to be raised before its current production plan is fully funded.

Samson's current timeline points to summer 2027. The company says it expects its Builder Assist assembly line to be ready by then. Its first year of production will focus mostly on customers who previously paid for some of the earliest delivery positions. Depositors and reservation holders would follow. Then there is the price. Samson currently estimates the Switchblade VFR kit will start at $200,000. The IFR version carries an estimated price of $235,000. Those prices can still change before customer production gets underway.

Bousfield tells CyberGuy that reaching this point has been part of the plan for years. "It's been great developing the technology for a flying car that you park in your garage and is high performance in both modes. Now we get to put it out for people to use and explore the world around them." Before that happens, buyers will have to do something you probably have never done when purchasing a car.

Buying a Switchblade comes with homework. Samson plans for the aircraft to operate under the Experimental Amateur-Built category in the U.S. FAA rules require the "major portion," meaning more than 50%, of an eligible amateur-built aircraft's fabrication and assembly to be completed by people building it for their own education or recreation. That requirement is often called the 51% rule.

Samson says its Builder Assist program will guide owners through their portion of the process. The company says much of its manufacturing process will be automated and computer-driven. It estimates an owner can finish the required work in as little as one week. One regulatory detail deserves some attention here. The FAA says it evaluates aircraft kits to determine whether they can allow a builder to meet the major-portion requirement. The FAA does not approve or certify the kit itself. The finished aircraft also goes through the FAA airworthiness process. So this will be a very different experience from walking into a dealership, signing a few forms and driving home.

A Switchblade may drive like a vehicle on the ground, but once those wings come out, aviation rules take over. Samson says you will need a private pilot certificate to fly one. Ground licensing can vary based on where you register the vehicle. The company says an automobile or motorcycle license may apply depending on local regulations. That also separates Switchblade from some of the other flying vehicles we have been following.

Electric air taxis such as Joby's eVTOL are designed around vertical takeoff and landing. Switchblade takes another route. It uses conventional runways but gives you something an air taxi cannot: the same vehicle stays with you after you land. That could be useful on a regional trip. Instead of landing and then finding a rental car or arranging another ride, you fold the wings away and keep going.

WISCONSIN MAN FLIES HELICOPTER TO CABELA'S BECAUSE THE DRIVE WAS TOO LONG

Here's what makes the Switchblade so interesting to me. You could pull out of your garage, drive to an airport, fly hundreds of miles and then keep driving after you land. No rental car. No waiting around for another ride. The same vehicle goes with you from start to finish. The new funding gets Samson closer to making that happen, but I would not start clearing space in the garage yet. The company still has to finish funding its production plans, choose where to build the Switchblade and put the latest version through more testing. We have seen an earlier prototype fly, but the redesigned vehicle heading toward production still needs to show what it can do in the air.

And if you are thinking, "Where do I sign up?" there is a lot more involved than the estimated $200,000 starting price. You will need pilot training and access to an airport. You also have to take part in the Builder Assist process. For me, the next big moment comes when this latest Switchblade leaves the runway. If it can deliver on the speed, range and transformation Samson is targeting, this flying sports car suddenly gets a whole lot more interesting.

What I like about the Switchblade is that the idea makes sense the minute you see how it works. You drive to the airport, fly to another city, fold the wings away after you land and keep going. The latest design makes that even more interesting because all that flight hardware disappears inside a vehicle you can park in your garage.

Of course, most of us are not shopping for a $200,000 flying sports car. The price alone puts the Switchblade out of reach for the majority of us, and becoming a pilot adds another wrinkle. But that does not mean you have to be a potential buyer to find this fascinating. I certainly am not planning to put one in my garage tomorrow, but I want to see whether Samson can actually pull this off.

The new funding gives Samson a much stronger push toward production, and we have already seen an earlier Switchblade fly. Now I want to see this redesigned version get into the air. If Samson can deliver what it is promising, we could be watching a pretty remarkable idea make the jump from a prototype we have followed for years to a flying sports car people can actually own.

Would you trust one vehicle to take you down the highway and into the sky, or would you want to see a few years of customer flights before climbing aboard? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
